correctness.rationale: For all d≥3, N≥1: f′(ζ_d^j)=dζ_d^(−j), so signed meridian shifts are exactly (2πi/d)sum a_jζ_d^j. The nonzero algebraic integer norm has two complex-conjugate factors |α|²; the other φ(d)−2 are ≤N, yielding the uniform lower bound. φ(d) independent powers furnish (L+1)^φ(d) distinct points in a square; a smaller-cell partition forces a nonzero difference of cost ≤φ(d)L and size at most 6sqrt(2)φ(d)L^(1−φ(d)/2). Choosing L=floor(N/φ(d)) and treating N<φ(d) yields the stated explicit upper bound. The φ(d)=2 cases have exact min 1, and rotational invariance turns existence of arbitrarily small shifts into full planar density. The checker ran successfully for finite examples but is not used as infinite proof.

value.rationale: The least nonzero meridian-word displacement is a natural finite-complexity invariant of an analytic-continuation surface with dense branching. The theorem determines its sharp budget exponent in every degree and a complete discrete/dense conductor dichotomy. This measures a quantitative obstruction to approaching nearby branch values that qualitative period-group closure does not specify. It can distinguish analytic continuation at finite winding budgets without requiring a broader downstream theorem.
